planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings or container stock in late spring in full sun to light shade with fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic soil; this cultivar is part of the Philippine 'Dona' breeding series named for First Ladies and is grown from cuttings rather than seed since the enlarged sepal clusters are sterile hybrid-derived traits.

directions: Grow as a large tropical shrub in full sun to partial shade on fertile, well-drained, humus-rich soil kept consistently moist during the warm growing season. Unlike the plain white-bracted species, 'Dona Aurora' produces fully doubled clusters of pure white, snowflake-shaped sepals that persist far longer on the plant than the small true flowers they surround, giving an especially dense, long-lasting floral display from late spring through fall. Prune hard after the coolest part of winter to encourage the flush of new growth that carries the heaviest bloom, and protect from frost since even brief chilling will defoliate or kill stems to the ground.

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings in late spring in full sun to partial shade with fertile, well-drained soil; named for Thailand's Queen Sirikit, this hybrid is propagated vegetatively since it does not come true from seed.

directions: Site in full sun to light afternoon shade in fertile, well-drained soil enriched with organic matter; this hybrid Mussaenda carries large clusters of soft pink, papery sepals surrounding the small true flowers, a color distinct from the white-bracted species sold as plain Mussaenda philippica. It flowers most heavily on new growth through the warm months, so periodic tip pruning after flushes keeps the shrub dense and encourages repeat bloom. Grow in a large container and overwinter indoors near a bright window outside zone 10-11, since it has no frost tolerance.
sources: LSU AgCenter — Tropical Ornamentals for Gulf Coast Landscapes

planting.note: Plant container-grown stock or rooted cuttings in spring in bright, filtered light with evenly moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil; this Brazilian understory shrub scorches in direct midday sun and prefers the dappled light of a shade house or patio.

directions: Grow in bright, indirect light or filtered shade in consistently moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil, as this Atlantic Forest native from Brazil is an understory shrub rather than a full-sun plant. The curious flowers hang like small candles, with a tubular cluster of deep red-violet petals that never fully opens emerging from a flared, bright red calyx, and they appear in flushes nearly year-round in warm, humid conditions. Pinch growing tips periodically to keep the naturally lanky stems bushy, and protect from any frost since it has no cold tolerance outside the tropics.
sources: North Carolina State University Extension — Pavonia multiflora

planting.note: Divide and pot offset bulbs in spring into shallow, wide containers using a fast-draining, sandy succulent mix; this dwarf form clumps readily and is almost always grown and sold as potted divisions rather than from seed.

directions: Pot in a fast-draining, sandy succulent mix in bright, indirect light or morning sun, and allow the surface to dry between waterings; this compact dwarf selection stays noticeably smaller and tighter in habit than standard Ledebouria socialis, with the same olive-green, purple-spotted leaves marked by a glossy silver overlay. Grow as a houseplant or patio succulent in cool-winter climates, bringing it indoors well before the first frost since the small bulbs have no cold hardiness. Repot and divide the crowded bulb clusters every year or two to maintain the dense, miniature clumping habit that makes this form popular for small pots and dish gardens.
sources: North Carolina State University Extension — Ledebouria socialis

planting.note: Plant container-grown specimens in spring in full sun to light shade with deep, well-drained soil; this weeping variety is propagated clonally by cuttings or air-layering to preserve its compact pendulous habit, since seedlings revert toward the tall columnar straight species.

directions: Plant in full sun to light shade in deep, well-drained soil with room for a dense, drooping crown of narrow, glossy, wavy-edged leaves that cascade from the branches on long, slender petioles. Unlike the straight species, which grows into a tall, strictly columnar avenue tree, this weeping variety stays considerably shorter and broader, making it better suited to screening, specimen planting, or smaller tropical gardens where the full-size mast tree would outgrow the space. Water regularly while establishing, then taper to occasional deep watering once the root system matures, and protect young plants from frost since the species has no cold tolerance.
